what_its_for: Glipizide is used to lower blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It works by helping your pancreas make more insulin, which helps your body use sugar properly. It is used along with a healthy diet and exercise to keep your blood sugar under control.
how_to_take: Take glipizide by mouth with a full glass of water. The regular tablet should be taken 30 minutes before a meal, usually breakfast. The extended-release tablet (Glucotrol XL) should be taken with breakfast. Swallow the extended-release tablet whole — do not crush, chew, or split it. Take your medicine at the same time every day to help you remember.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it based on how well your blood sugar is controlled. The usual starting dose for the regular tablet is 5 mg once daily. The maximum dose is 40 mg per day, split into two doses. For the extended-release tablet, the usual starting dose is 5 mg once daily, with a maximum of 20 mg per day. Always follow your doctor's instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is close to mealtime. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store glipizide at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use medicine past the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking glipizide — it can cause your blood sugar to drop too low or rise too high, and can cause flushing, nausea, or headache. Avoid skipping meals, as this can cause low blood sugar. Limit sugary foods and drinks. Be careful with prolonged sun exposure, as glipizide can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight — wear sunscreen and protective clothing. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and herbal supplements, as many can affect your blood sugar.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you have signs of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), such as shaking, sweating, dizziness, fast heartbeat, blurred vision, sudden hunger, or confusion. Also call your doctor if you have signs of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia), such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision. Seek emergency care for severe allergic reactions such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Tell your doctor if you are sick, having surgery, or under unusual stress, as your blood sugar may be harder to control.
when_it_works: Glipizide starts lowering blood sugar within 30 minutes of taking a dose. However, it may take several days to a few weeks before you see the full benefit in your blood sugar levels. Keep taking your medicine even if you feel well. Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition, and this medicine works best when combined with a healthy diet and regular exercise.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): You may be more sensitive to the blood sugar-lowering effects of glipizide, which means a higher risk of low blood sugar. Your doctor will likely start you on a lower dose. Kidney or liver problems: These conditions can affect how your body processes glipizide and may increase the risk of low blood sugar. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or choose a different medicine. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Glipizide is generally not recommended during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor about the safest options to manage your blood sugar during this time. Children: Glipizide is not approved for use in children.
